uses: Chamomile has been part of folk practice since the days of ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome. The flowers are traditionally brewed as a bedtime tea for restlessness and an unsettled stomach, and in many homes it was the first cup offered for a cold. A cooled infusion has long been used as a mouth rinse or a gentle wash for the skin. Old herbals also describe the flowers in warm baths and compresses for tired, aching bodies.
energetics: Culpeper called garden chamomile hot and dry in the first degree, a gentle warmth
caution_pregnancy: Little is known about the safety of chamomile during pregnancy or breastfeeding, so ask a health care provider first. The EMA treats the plain dried flower as a tea as acceptable in pregnancy and nursing, but does not recommend chamomile extracts or tinctures then because there isn't enough data. If you use a chamomile cream on the nipples, wipe it off before nursing so the baby doesn't become sensitized.
caution_medications: Interactions with the blood thinner warfarin have been reported. Early studies suggest chamomile may make birth control pills less effective. It may also affect drugs the liver breaks down; such interactions were reported in kidney transplant patients taking large amounts for about two months. It could add to the effect of sedatives. Talk with a pharmacist or doctor before using it alongside any medicine.
caution_conditions: Avoid it if you are allergic to ragweed, chrysanthemums, marigolds, daisies or other plants in the daisy family (Asteraceae). Serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, have happened. Chamomile may act a little like estrogen, so anyone with an estrogen-sensitive condition such as breast or uterine cancer should ask their doctor first. The tea isn't advised for babies under 6 months. Full chamomile baths aren't advised with open wounds, acute skin disease, high fever, severe infection, or serious heart or circulation problems.
caution_duration: Tea-sized amounts are considered likely safe. For medicinal use, safety has only been described for short-term use. The EMA advises seeing a practitioner if symptoms last more than a week.
caution_topical: Can cause allergic skin reactions, especially in people sensitive to the daisy family. Keep it away from the eyes, where it may cause irritation.
garden_harvest_timing: Snip the flower heads when they are close to full bloom, through the season; keep picking for more flowers.
garden_water: Keep the top layer of soil moist but not soggy; the roots are shallow.
notes: An easy annual that self-seeds readily unless every flower head is picked. Culpeper's own chamomile was the related Roman chamomile; he recorded that the Egyptians dedicated it to the Sun. Grieve notes the old garden belief that chamomile helps ailing plants nearby, hence its nickname.
